claims.text: Thermally activated kink-pair nucleation and migration on screw dislocations is the dominant yielding mechanism in single-crystal FeNiCrMn.
Yielding in single-crystal FeNiCrMn is not dominated by dislocation nucleation at specific defects.
Phase transformation is not the dominant mechanism at the onset of yielding in single-crystal FeNiCrMn.
The initial FeNiCrMn single crystal is an FCC solid solution.
The initial alloy is free of precipitates and secondary phases.
Fe, Ni, Cr, and Mn are randomly distributed in the initial crystal.
Atomic-size differences among the constituent elements cause severe local lattice distortion in FeNiCrMn.
Local lattice distortion creates friction that impedes dislocation motion and strengthens the alloy.
The friction generated by lattice distortion necessitates kink-pair nucleation for screw-dislocation glide in FCC FeNiCrMn.
Kink-pair formation is the rate-limiting step for screw-dislocation motion in the low-to-middle stress regime.
A high kink-pair formation barrier makes dislocation velocity strongly temperature sensitive.
Thermally activated kink-pair motion makes yielding relatively insensitive to strain rate in the low-to-middle stress regime.
Yield strength decreases strongly as temperature increases from 77 K toward 600 K.
Yield strength varies minimally over strain rates from approximately 10^-4 s^-1 to 10^2 s^-1.
No FCC-to-BCC transformation occurs during the initial yielding event.
The stress-strain curve exhibits a smooth thermally activated-glide transition rather than abrupt phase-transformation softening.
At sufficiently high strain rates, dislocation motion may transition from kink-pair control to phonon-drag control.
Using a single crystal eliminates grain-boundary effects.
Traditional FCC metals such as pure Ni or Fe generally have greater yield-strength strain-rate sensitivity because they have lower lattice distortion and different dislocation-drag mechanisms.
